title: The thread that won't break
hook: such a thread doesn't break, burn, get dirty or wear out (Asa di Var, ang 471)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the janeu, and your line: compassion is the thread. Did you keep a string in your pocket? Today, the second half of that same salok, and four things the thread of the soul can survive. Day five hundred fifty-five.

Open any drawer at home and you'll find something that wore out. A sweater with elbows gone thin. A phone cable split near the plug. A favorite shirt washed one too many times. Everything made of fiber frays eventually. Cotton breaks under strain. It burns in a second near a flame. It picks up stains. And even if you protect it from all of that, time thins it out. Guru Nanak knew all four of those ways a thread can fail, and he named them, one by one, about the thread of compassion we tied yesterday.
screen: `A SWEATER WITH THIN ELBOWS.` → `EVERY FIBER FRAYS.` → `FOUR WAYS A THREAD FAILS.`

segments.voice: Here's how the salok on ang 471 continues, in paraphrase. Such a thread doesn't break. It doesn't get dirty. It doesn't burn. It isn't lost. Blessed, Nanak says, are the people who go about wearing it around their necks. Four nots. One way to hear them: breaking is strain: the hard week, the argument, the shock. Dirt is the slow grime of daily life: resentment, envy, gossip. Burning is the sudden fire: rage, disaster, loss. And being lost is time itself, the way things simply slip away. A cotton thread can't survive any of these for long. A thread spun from compassion, contentment, restraint and truth, the salok says, survives all four. Then Guru Nanak looks at the outer thread with plain eyes. It's bought for a few coins, he says, and put on in a ceremony. And when the body dies, it falls away; the person leaves without it. Whatever is tied to the body goes the way of the body. The next salok in the var adds a line that answers it. Through trust in the Name, honor arises, and praise of the One is the true thread. Worn that way, it doesn't break in the Court of the Lord. Sikh teaching reads this as a question about what goes with us. Not possessions, not status, not even the symbols we're given. What goes is what we've become. A grandmother who has worn that thread for decades, patient at the stove, honest at the market, takes it with her. The cotton one stays behind.
screen: `IT WON'T BREAK, STAIN, BURN, OR BE LOST.` · `THE OUTER THREAD FALLS AWAY.` · `PRAISE IS THE TRUE THREAD.` · `WHAT GOES IS WHAT WE'VE BECOME.` · then, large: `IT WON'T WEAR OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think what in you won't wear out. Sit and breathe slowly. Picture yourself many years from now, much older, with most of today's worries long gone. Ask: what in me will still be there? Not a job title. Not a look. Maybe a way of listening. A patience you've been building. A love for certain people. Let one quality come forward. Picture it as a thread, already strong, getting stronger. If you pray, you can say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Compassion, one strand of the soul's thread: in Guru Nanak's salok, spun with contentment, restraint and truth, it doesn't break, get dirty, burn, or get lost, and it goes with you.
Your line: it won't wear out. Today, when something breaks or frays, a cable, a plan, your patience, say the line and give a minute to the quality you named. Day five hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikh teaching holds that virtues and the praise of the One are what go with a person beyond death.

fork.setup: you're holding two threads: one cotton, one spun from compassion and truth. after a lifetime, which one is still with you?
options: the cotton one, if you're careful.
the one of compassion and truth.
fork.reveal: the outer thread falls away when the body dies. the thread of the soul doesn't break, burn, get dirty or get lost.

trapdoor: what you thought: a thread that won't break is just a nice image.
what it means: four failures, breaking, dirt, fire, loss, that a thread of virtue survives, while the outer thread goes with the body.
what a scholar hears: 'naa eh tutai naa mal lagai naa eh jalai na jaa-e'; the next salok makes praise, saalaahee, the true thread.

notes: The salok is paraphrased; confirm the four nots and 'dhan so maanas Nanakaa jo gal chale paa-e', and the lines about the outer thread (bought for a few cowries, put on in the square, falls off at death, departs without it).
The following salok ('naa-e maniai pat oopjai saalaahee sach soot / dargah andar paaeeai tag na tootas poot') paraphrased; confirm attribution and ang.
Care taken not to disparage the janeu; the description of the outer thread is kept to what the salok says. Confirm tone.
Original set to null: the day's word is an English phrase with no single Gurmukhi term.

Audit (10% sample): the four-failures reading is now marked as one way to hear the salok, and the unsupported closing claim that the thread 'grows stronger the longer it's worn' was replaced with a concrete picture.
